rv.q: Fierce new Eva Perón seduces again.
Grandage's vigorous direction and the vitality of the performances more than compensate for the unevenness of the material.
This is a big, fat, juicy blockbuster of a show.
This "Evita," starting with a dazzling sequence during the song "What's New, Buenos Aires," is the most impressive work New York has yet seen from Ashford.
And yet there's something distancing about this "Evita."
This bio-operetta begins and ends with the funeral of its title character.

So, there was an unexpected and exhilarating comfort to discover new joys in the decades-old touchstone, a high-point in the re-conceived “Evita” that tangoes its way to the Marquis Theatre this month, with Elena Roger in the title role.
One can't help but lean in, desperate for more.
And it was worth the ass-busting.
Although Roger evokes Evita's fiery personality, she does not have the belting vocal power to handle the challenging role - and her singing is often strained.
Despite the basic proficiency of the staging, it all feels too safe.
All her garish shenanigans are eerily rendered in chiaroscuro through the billowing clouds of mist and moody, monumentalist settings in Michael Grandage’s fevered production.
On that level, Evita succeeds brilliantly.
As a study of the falseness of character, and the narcissism of benevolence, it’s a transfixing study, one which endears us to a character we’re loath to love.
Roger is often flat and shrill and has trouble enunciating some of the words (due in part to her actual Argentine accent).
But the revival, the first on Broadway since the show debuted in 1979, is a sadly missed opportunity.
Put it all together and we get a sort of Evita Bland.
This Evita never quite wins through, and it’s a shame, because she’s surrounded by plenty of peripheral promise.
Haven’t we outgrown this bloated extravaganza?
Today the story of an ambitious woman using her sexuality to get ahead seems trite and quaint.

tn.cat: Best Featured Actor in a Musical

cn.t: Ricky Martin's charismatic star turn overshadows a mixed revival that critics find lacking the danger and vocal power of the original, with Elena Roger's performance dividing opinion despite her emotional authenticity.

sg.ra: Closest and most direct view of the stage at Marquis Theatre, with the fullest sound. The standard top pick for any show here.
An elevated, full-stage view with no orchestra-level neck-craning — especially strong for shows with big staging or choreography.
A modest side angle on the stage but still close and clear — a reliable choice when center seats are sold out.
Farther from the stage than center orchestra — less up-close, but the sound still carries well.
At 1,611 seats, Marquis Theatre is one of the larger Broadway houses — far side mezzanine seats sit well off-axis and a long way from the stage.

vs.sum: The Marquis Theatre offers excellent comfort with spacious seating and good sightlines from most areas, although the ambiance is somewhat lacking due to its modern, hotel-integrated design. Facilities are well-equipped with ample restrooms and concessions, making it a convenient choice for theatergoers.

acc.note: Elevator via Marriott Marquis hotel. 10 wheelchair spaces. No elevator to Mezzanine.
